deep.reconstruction:
Context: on the previous page (229r) Riemann studies rational interpolation. A rational function u = Σa_m x^m / Σb_m x^m is required to take prescribed values u_μ at 2n nodes x_μ. He writes the numerator and denominator as alternating sums over splittings of the nodes into a set τ of n−1 nodes and a set σ of n+1 nodes (Jacobi's determinantal solution). He then puts f_1(x)=Π(x−α) over one class of nodes (α_ν) and f_2(x)=Π(x−β) over the other (β_μ), with data g_1(α_ν), g_2(β_μ). He also writes the ratio of the term obtained by exchanging one α_ν with one β_μ to the base term, and tries integral forms of these sums.

This page, line by line:

(1) u = Σ a_m x^m / Σ b_m x^m. The interpolation conditions are the homogeneous linear system Σ_m b_m x_μ^m u_μ − Σ_m a_m x_μ^m = 0 for every node μ.

(2) A double-exchange ratio, generalising the single exchange on 229r. Swapping two α's (α_ν, α_ρ) with two β's (β_μ, β_π) multiplies the base term by
[g_2(β_μ) g_2(β_π) / (g_1(α_ν) g_1(α_ρ))] · [Π*(β_μ−α) Π*(β_π−α) (x−α_ν)(x−α_ρ) Π*(α_ν−β) Π*(α_ρ−β)] / [Π*(α_ν−α) Π*(α_ρ−α) (x−β_μ)(x−β_π) Π*(β_μ−β) Π*(β_π−β)].
Here * means the vanishing factor is omitted, i.e. these are essentially f_1'(α), f_2'(β) and so on. The cancelled factors (β_μ−β_π) and (α_ν−α_ρ) show him adjusting the cross terms.

(3) He tries to write such double sums as (contour-type) integrals by replacing the discrete exchanged node with a continuous variable:
∫ g_2(t) f_1(t) (t−t_1) dt / [(x−t)(t−α_ν)^2 (t−α_ρ)^2 f_2(t)] · g_2(t_1) f_1(t_1) dt_1 / [(x−t_1)(t_1−α_ν)^2 (t_1−α_ρ)^2 f_2(t_1)].
The companion integral is ∫ (x−s_1) f_2(s)(s−s_1) ds / [g_1(s) f_1(s)] · (x−s_1) f_2(s_1) ds_1 / [g_1(s_1) f_1(s_1)]. Presumably the residues at the zeros of f_2 (resp. f_1) are meant to reproduce the sums over exchanges. The factor (t−t_1) is the continuous analogue of the omitted difference of the two exchanged nodes. My reading of the intended residue mechanism is a reconstruction, not certain.

(4) He abandons that and switches to a Laplace-integral representation of the squared reciprocal factors (cf. (β_μ−α_ν)^2 on 229r, Cauchy-determinant type products). Gauss's Π(1)=Γ(2)=1 gives
∫_0^∞ e^{−(k_{μν}+(t_μ−s_ν)i) y_{μν}} y_{μν} dy_{μν} = Π(1)/(k_{μν}+(t_μ−s_ν)i)^2.
Here k_{μν}>0 is a regulariser that makes the oscillatory integral converge; the case k→0 recovers 1/(i(t_μ−s_ν))^2.

(5) Multiplying over all pairs (μ,ν) gives an integral over the matrix y=(y_{μν})≥0 with weight Π y_{μν}. The exponential factors as e^{−Σk_{μν}y_{μν}} times e^{(±) i Σ_μ t_μ Σ_ν y_{μν}} times e^{∓ i Σ_ν s_ν Σ_μ y_{μν}}. So t_μ couples only to the row sum Σ_ν y_{μν}, and s_ν only to the column sum Σ_μ y_{μν}.

(6) Hence if the product is integrated against functions of the t's and s's, the t- and s-integrations become Fourier transforms evaluated at the margins. He names these φ_μ = φ(Σ_ν y_{μν}) and ψ_ν = ψ(Σ_μ y_{μν}). The whole expression becomes
∫_0^∞ e^{−Σ k y} [Δ?] φ φ' φ'' … ψ ψ' ψ'' … Π dy_{μν}.

(7) He then introduces the margins as new variables, Σ_ν y_{μν} = s_μ and Σ_μ y_{μν} = t_ν. These satisfy the single linear relation Σ s_μ − Σ t_ν = 0, both sides being the total Σ y_{μν}. This is the constraint defining a transportation polytope; it is the natural next step toward integrating out the y's at fixed margins.

The page breaks off here. Its purpose is to obtain integral representations of the Jacobi/Cauchy-type sums arising in rational interpolation, via exponential (Schwinger-type) parametrisation of the reciprocal squared differences.
errors: Sign inconsistency: the integrand exponent is −i(t_μ−s_ν)y, i.e. −i t_μ y + i s_ν y, but the factorised exponentials are written e^{+ i t_μ Σ_ν y_{μν}} and e^{− i s_ν Σ_μ y_{μν}}. The signs are reversed (harmless if consistently conjugated, but a slip as written).

Notation reuse/swap: in the exponent t_μ goes with the row sum Σ_ν y_{μν}, yet the last lines define Σ_ν y_{μν} = s_μ and Σ_μ y_{μν} = t_ν. The margins are thus relabelled with the opposite letters, and s, t were already used earlier on the page as integration variables.
The Laplace formula requires Re(k_{μν})>0. It is valid as written with real k>0; the role of k as a convergence factor is implicit.

The contour-integral versions in (3) are left incomplete: limits, contour and normalisation are not given, and some factors are overwritten. They cannot be confirmed as correct identities from the page alone.

deep.surprise_reason: The ingredients are classical: rational interpolation à la Cauchy–Jacobi, and the Euler/Laplace integral for 1/a^2. Riemann's habitual Fourier/Laplace technique makes their combination natural for him. The mildly notable feature is the systematic exponential parametrisation of a whole bipartite product Π 1/(k+i(t_μ−s_ν))^2. This reduces the s, t dependence to row and column margins of a matrix of auxiliary variables, a device reminiscent of later Schwinger/Feynman parametrisations and transportation-polytope integrals. However, it is a fragmentary, unfinished sketch with no result drawn.

Sum of row sums equals sum of column sums (Σ s_μ − Σ t_ν = 0)
